title: Madagascar flying foxes are getting smaller
verification: Smithsonian report read in full; the journal article page is the primary study. Facts used: 121 specimens, nine museums, about 150 years, 12 skull/tooth features, skulls about 6% longer before the 1980s, population estimates and IUCN vulnerable status, one pup a year. The report stresses hunting is a suspected, unproven cause; wording kept to 'may'.

caption:
The biggest fruit bats in Madagascar are getting smaller.

The Malagasy flying fox (Pteropus rufus) has a wingspan of up to five feet. Researchers at the Field Museum in Chicago, Emily Cornelius Ruhs and Steven Goodman, measured 12 features of the skulls and teeth of 121 specimens held by nine museums in the United States and Europe, collected over roughly 150 years. Bats collected before the 1980s had skulls about 6% longer than those collected afterward.

The drop lines up with the rise of commercial hunting, when the bats became easier to find in markets and restaurants. The authors say that does not prove hunting is the cause, and climate change and forest loss may play a part too. Ruhs says the concern is that hunters are removing sexually mature, reproductively active bats from the population.

That matters because flying foxes are keystone seed spreaders that help forests regrow, and a female has only one pup a year. An estimated 300,000 lived on the island in the early 2000s, and reports suggest about two-thirds have been lost. Researchers still don't know whether the change is genetic.
